consent_form.title: Consent form
paragraphs: I am Kexin Que, a researcher in the Department of Psychology at Northwestern University. You are reading this document because you selected our study from Prolific. You are invited to take part in a research study of the basic psychological processes that people engage in to make sense of and understand the world around them. The purpose of this research study is to understand how people think about the structure of number words. If you agree to participate, you will be asked to play a fun game about finding the correct number words in a novel language.

Participation in this study will involve no cost to you. Payment will be provided in accordance with Prolific’s payment policies. You will receive a $1 bonus if your performance is above 80%. Payment will be processed through Prolific. The experiment is expected to last no more than 20 minutes. Taking part in this study may help scientists to understand the difficulties involved in learning a domain of mathematics or science. Your participation does not involve any risks other than what you would encounter in daily life. You may leave the study at any time.

Confidentiality: Study records that can identify you will be kept confidential because we will not request any identifiable data. This survey is being hosted by Prolific and involves a secure connection.

The results of the research study may be published, but your name will not be used. If you have any questions about this study you may contact Lance Rips, the person in charge of this research study; you can also contact Kexin Que (see contact information below). If you have questions about your rights as a research subject, you can contact the Northwestern University Institutional Review Board (IRB) Office. You can call them at (312) 503-9338 or send e-mail to irb@northwestern.edu. If you want a copy of this consent for your records, you can print it from the screen. If you would like any documentation related to this research study, please email your request to the Principal Investigator at rips@northwestern.edu.
If you wish to participate, please select the Accept button below to begin the survey. If you do not wish to participate in this study, please close this webpage.

Sincerely,
Lance Rips

instruction_pages.body:
In this experiment, we’d like you to pretend that you are an anthropologist studying alien languages. This time, you have been assigned to study a population called the Numerons. Your job is to figure out some aspects of the Numerons’ number language.

Below are some things you’ve already discovered about their number language. Please study them carefully.
1. There are two kinds of one-word number words in Numerons’ number language: Digits and Powers.

Digits are words for small numbers. They represent any numeral word up to the value of the base number. In English, they could be any of the numbers below ten (one, two,…, nine). However, the base of the Numerons’ number language is unknown and may not conform to your own number base.

So far, we have only discovered two Digits: “Fim” and “Miv”. It is unknown whether Fim is greater than Miv or vice versa. They are just two of possibly many more Digits.

Powers are words for some special large numbers. They are mainly nounlike number words. They are like thousand, billion, and other similar kinds of number words in English. Remember, the base of the Numerons’ number language is unknown and may not conform to your own number base.

So far, we have discovered five powers: “Pog,” “Gom,” “Jop,” “Zok,” and “Lod.” Lod is greater than Zok, Zok is greater than Jop, Jop is greater than Gom, and Gom is greater than Pog. These are just five of possibly many more powers.
instruction_pages.notes: Powers: Pog, Gom, Jop, Zok, Lod (ranked from small to large)

instruction_pages.body: 2. Number words in the Numeron language refer to positive whole numbers.
3. The Numerons’ number words are made by using a set of one-word number words and combining them to produce more complex numbers.

4. The number words are words used in the Numerons’ natural language (like “four” or “seventy-two” in English). They are NOT number symbols, such as the Arabic or Roman numerals (such as “4,” “IV,” “72,” or “LXXII”).

magnitude_instructions:
As a professional anthropologist, you must demonstrate a good understanding of what is already known about the Numerons’ number language. Starting on the next page, you will see one pair of power words at a time and judge their relative magnitudes. You must answer at least 18 out of 20 comparisons correctly (90% accuracy) to move on to the next task. If you score below 90%, you will repeat the set of 20 comparisons. Please try to memorize the relative magnitudes of the power words without taking notes or using other aids.

On the next pages, you will see statements such as “Lod > Zok.” Decide whether the first word is greater than the second. Press C for No or / for Yes. Make each judgment as quickly and accurately as you can.

Study the relative magnitudes of the Numerons’ words—for example, Lod is greater than Zok. When you have memorized the relative magnitudes of the Powers, press Right Key to continue.

task_pages.body: Starting on the next page, you will see one number expression at a time. Your job is to decide whether it is a real number word in the Numerons’ language. In your own native language, for example, not all combinations of number words when placed together form another number word. If X is a number word and Y is a number word, the combinations XX, YY, XY, and YX may or may not be number words. Only certain combinations are real number words.

Please remember to study them carefully and then decide if they are a real number word. 

Press / for Yes or C for No. Respond as quickly as you can while trying to be correct.

The first trial starts in the next page.

judgment_prompt: Is the number expression below a real number word in the Numerons’ language?

emphasize: Quadrillion is the largest known single-word power in this language.

english_instruction_pages.body:
Your new task is to study a novel language that borrows words from English to express numbers.

So far, you have discovered seven power words in this language, ordered from smallest to largest:

Powers: ten, hundred, thousand, million, billion, trillion, quadrillion (ranked from small to large)

These words have the same numerical values as in English. Quadrillion is the largest known single-word power in this language. No single-word powers for larger values have been discovered.
emphasize: Quadrillion is the largest known single-word power in this language.

english_instruction_pages.body:

Press / for Yes or C for No. Respond as quickly and accurately as you can.
